titre: A Bank Collapses Between Two Time Zones, and Basel Is Born
accroche: On June 26, 1974, a Cologne bank closes at 4:30 p.m., having received marks but not yet paid back the dollars owed in New York, where it is only 10:30 a.m.
contenu_vulgarise:
On June 26, 1974, the West German banking authorities withdraw the license of Bankhaus Herstatt of Cologne, a mid-sized institution brought down by reckless bets on currencies. The decision comes at 4:30 p.m., Frankfurt time. That day, dozens of banks around the world have already transferred German marks to Herstatt in exchange for U.S. dollars that it owed them in return, in New York, where it is still only 10:30 in the morning. Those dollars will never come. Herstatt closed between the two halves of a single transaction.

## A Risk With No Name

What strikes bankers is not the failure itself: a bank piling up 470 million marks in losses against 44 million marks in capital could not survive. It is the mechanism that turns a local failure into international losses. A currency trade settles in two steps, in two countries, often in two different time zones. Until both payments have been made, one side remains exposed without knowing it, at the mercy of a collapse that occurs between the two payments. This settlement risk takes the name of the bank that revealed it to the whole world: “Herstatt risk.”

At the end of 1974, the central bank governors of the Group of Ten, meeting at the Bank for International Settlements in Basel, create a standing committee so that the banking supervisors of several countries can finally talk to one another. Its first meeting is held in February 1975. This committee will later take the name Basel Committee on Banking Supervision.

## The Shift

No country alone could have prevented another Herstatt: the risk was born precisely from the coexistence of several banking jurisdictions that coordinated nothing among themselves. Banking supervision, until then a strictly national matter, with a bank answerable only to the oversight of its own country, becomes from 1974 a permanent forum for cooperation among supervisors. None of them gives up the slightest portion of sovereignty in doing so: the Basel Committee has never had the power to compel a member country, only that of bringing the way each one oversees its own banks into convergence, through discussion and the publication of common rules.

repere.texte: Bankhaus Herstatt of Cologne piles up 470 million marks in losses against 44 million marks in capital before the West German authorities withdraw its license on June 26, 1974, at 4:30 p.m. Frankfurt time, or 10:30 a.m. in New York, where the dollars owed in return will never be paid.

carte.punch: A bank closed between two payments of the same transaction. The banking world got organized.
carte.idee: On June 26, 1974, the German bank Herstatt closes after receiving marks from its counterparties, but before paying back the dollars owed in New York. The episode gives rise, in Basel, to the standing banking supervision committee that still exists today.

quiz.question: What is the “Herstatt risk” revealed by the 1974 failure?
choix: The risk that a central bank refuses to act as lender of last resort to a bank in difficulty
The risk that one of the two legs of an international payment is paid without the other being paid
The risk that a country devalues its currency without warning its trading partners
The risk that a bank lends more than its own funds allow
quiz.explication: Herstatt closed after receiving the marks owed to it but before paying the dollars due in return in New York, leaving its counterparties exposed without knowing it between the two payments.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What ratio of losses to capital did Herstatt show before its license was withdrawn?
choix: 44 million marks in losses against 470 million marks in capital
470 million marks in losses against 44 million marks in capital
Losses equal to its capital, a balance only just broken
No measurable losses: the license was withdrawn for administrative reasons
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry states that Herstatt was piling up 470 million marks in losses against only 44 million marks in capital, an imbalance that made failure inevitable.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who creates, at the end of 1974, the standing committee that will become the Basel Committee?
choix: The European Parliament, at Germany's request
The central bank governors of the Group of Ten
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry states that the central bank governors of the Group of Ten, meeting at the Bank for International Settlements, create this standing committee.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What power does the Basel Committee have over member countries, according to the entry?
choix: The power to suspend the banking license of an offending country
The power to lift financial sanctions against a member state
The power to impose its decisions directly on national banks
No power of compulsion: only cooperation and common rules
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry states that the Basel Committee has never had the power to compel a member country, only that of bringing practices into convergence through discussion.
